XIX.


The day was fresh, with a lively spring wind full of dust. All the old
ladies in both families had got out their faded sables and yellowing
ermines, and the smell of camphor from the front pews almost smothered
the faint spring scent of the lilies banking the altar.

Newland Archer, at a signal from the sexton, had come out of the vestry
and placed himself with his best man on the chancel step of Grace
Church.

The signal meant that the brougham bearing the bride and her father
was in sight; but there was sure to be a considerable interval of
adjustment and consultation in the lobby, where the bridesmaids were
already hovering like a cluster of Easter blossoms. During this
unavoidable lapse of time the bridegroom, in proof of his eagerness,
was expected to expose himself alone to the gaze of the assembled
company; and Archer had gone through this formality as resignedly as
through all the others which made of a nineteenth century New York
wedding a rite that seemed to belong to the dawn of history. Everything
was equally easy--or equally painful, as one chose to put it--in
the path he was committed to tread, and he had obeyed the flurried
injunctions of his best man as piously as other bridegrooms had obeyed
his own, in the days when he had guided them through the same labyrinth.

So far he was reasonably sure of having fulfilled all his obligations.
The bridesmaids' eight bouquets of white lilac and lilies-of-the-valley
had been sent in due time, as well as the gold and sapphire
sleeve-links of the eight ushers and the best man's cat's-eye
scarf-pin; Archer had sat up half the night trying to vary the wording
of his thanks for the last batch of presents from men friends and
ex-lady-loves; the fees for the Bishop and the Rector were safely in
the pocket of his best man; his own luggage was already at Mrs. Manson
Mingott's, where the wedding-breakfast was to take place, and so were
the travelling clothes into which he was to change; and a private
compartment had been engaged in the train that was to carry the young
couple to their unknown destination--concealment of the spot in which
the bridal night was to be spent being one of the most sacred taboos of
the prehistoric ritual.

"Got the ring all right?" whispered young van der Luyden Newland, who
was inexperienced in the duties of a best man, and awed by the weight
of his responsibility.

Archer made the gesture which he had seen so many bridegrooms make:
with his ungloved right hand he felt in the pocket of his dark grey
waistcoat, and assured himself that the little gold circlet (engraved
inside: _Newland to May, April ——, 187—_) was in its place; then,
resuming his former attitude, his tall hat and pearl-grey gloves with
black stitchings grasped in his left hand, he stood looking at the door
of the church.

Overhead, Handel's March swelled pompously through the imitation stone
vaulting, carrying on its waves the faded drift of the many weddings
at which, with cheerful indifference, he had stood on the same chancel
step watching other brides float up the nave toward other bridegrooms.

"How like a first night at the Opera!" he thought, recognising all
the same faces in the same boxes (no, pews), and wondering if, when
the Last Trump sounded, Mrs. Selfridge Merry would be there with the
same towering ostrich feathers in her bonnet, and Mrs. Beaufort with
the same diamond earrings and the same smile--and whether suitable
proscenium seats were already prepared for them in another world.

After that there was still time to review, one by one, the familiar
countenances in the first rows; the women's sharp with curiosity
and excitement, the men's sulky with the obligation of having to
put on their frock-coats before luncheon, and fight for food at the
wedding-breakfast.

"Too bad the breakfast is at old Catherine's," the bridegroom could
fancy Reggie Chivers saying. "But I'm told that Lovell Mingott insisted
on its being cooked by his own chef, so it ought to be good if one can
only get at it." And he could imagine Sillerton Jackson adding with
authority: "My dear fellow, haven't you heard? It's to be served at
small tables, in the new English fashion."

Archer's eyes lingered a moment on the left-hand pew, where his mother,
who had entered the church on Mr. Henry van der Luyden's arm, sat
weeping softly under her Chantilly veil, her hands in her grandmother's
ermine muff.

"Poor Janey!" he thought, looking at his sister, "even by screwing her
head around she can see only the people in the few front pews; and
they're mostly dowdy Newlands and Dagonets."

On the hither side of the white ribbon dividing off the seats reserved
for the families he saw Beaufort, tall and redfaced, scrutinising the
women with his arrogant stare. Beside him sat his wife, all silvery
chinchilla and violets; and on the far side of the ribbon, Lawrence
Lefferts's sleekly brushed head seemed to mount guard over the
invisible deity of "Good Form" who presided at the ceremony.

Archer wondered how many flaws Lefferts's keen eyes would discover
in the ritual of his divinity; then he suddenly recalled that he
too had once thought such questions important. The things that had
filled his days seemed now like a nursery parody of life, or like the
wrangles of mediaeval schoolmen over metaphysical terms that nobody
had ever understood. A stormy discussion as to whether the wedding
presents should be "shown" had darkened the last hours before the
wedding; and it seemed inconceivable to Archer that grown-up people
should work themselves into a state of agitation over such trifles,
and that the matter should have been decided (in the negative) by Mrs.
Welland's saying, with indignant tears: "I should as soon turn the
reporters loose in my house." Yet there was a time when Archer had had
definite and rather aggressive opinions on all such problems, and when
everything concerning the manners and customs of his little tribe had
seemed to him fraught with world-wide significance.

"And all the while, I suppose," he thought, "real people were living
somewhere, and real things happening to them ..."

"_There they come!_" breathed the best man excitedly; but the bridegroom
knew better.

The cautious opening of the door of the church meant only that Mr.
Brown the livery-stable keeper (gowned in black in his intermittent
character of sexton) was taking a preliminary survey of the scene
before marshalling his forces. The door was softly shut again; then
after another interval it swung majestically open, and a murmur ran
through the church: "The family!"

Mrs. Welland came first, on the arm of her eldest son. Her large pink
face was appropriately solemn, and her plum-coloured satin with pale
blue side-panels, and blue ostrich plumes in a small satin bonnet,
met with general approval; but before she had settled herself with a
stately rustle in the pew opposite Mrs. Archer's the spectators were
craning their necks to see who was coming after her. Wild rumours had
been abroad the day before to the effect that Mrs. Manson Mingott, in
spite of her physical disabilities, had resolved on being present at
the ceremony; and the idea was so much in keeping with her sporting
character that bets ran high at the clubs as to her being able to walk
up the nave and squeeze into a seat. It was known that she had insisted
on sending her own carpenter to look into the possibility of taking
down the end panel of the front pew, and to measure the space between
the seat and the front; but the result had been discouraging, and for
one anxious day her family had watched her dallying with the plan
of being wheeled up the nave in her enormous Bath chair and sitting
enthroned in it at the foot of the chancel.

The idea of this monstrous exposure of her person was so painful to her
relations that they could have covered with gold the ingenious person
who suddenly discovered that the chair was too wide to pass between
the iron uprights of the awning which extended from the church door to
the curbstone. The idea of doing away with this awning, and revealing
the bride to the mob of dressmakers and newspaper reporters who stood
outside fighting to get near the joints of the canvas, exceeded even
old Catherine's courage, though for a moment she had weighed the
possibility. "Why, they might take a photograph of my child and _put it
in the papers_!" Mrs. Welland exclaimed when her mother's last plan was
hinted to her; and from this unthinkable indecency the clan recoiled
with a collective shudder. The ancestress had had to give in; but her
concession was bought only by the promise that the wedding-breakfast
should take place under her roof, though (as the Washington Square
connection said) with the Wellands' house in easy reach it was hard to
have to make a special price with Brown to drive one to the other end
of nowhere.

Though all these transactions had been widely reported by the Jacksons
a sporting minority still clung to the belief that old Catherine would
appear in church, and there was a distinct lowering of the temperature
when she was found to have been replaced by her daughter-in-law.
Mrs. Lovell Mingott had the high colour and glassy stare induced
in ladies of her age and habit by the effort of getting into a new
dress; but once the disappointment occasioned by her mother-in-law's
non-appearance had subsided, it was agreed that her black Chantilly
over lilac satin, with a bonnet of Parma violets, formed the happiest
contrast to Mrs. Welland's blue and plum-colour. Far different was
the impression produced by the gaunt and mincing lady who followed on
Mr. Mingott's arm, in a wild dishevelment of stripes and fringes and
floating scarves; and as this last apparition glided into view Archer's
heart contracted and stopped beating.

He had taken it for granted that the Marchioness Manson was still in
Washington, where she had gone some four weeks previously with her
niece, Madame Olenska. It was generally understood that their abrupt
departure was due to Madame Olenska's desire to remove her aunt from
the baleful eloquence of Dr. Agathon Carver, who had nearly succeeded
in enlisting her as a recruit for the Valley of Love; and in the
circumstances no one had expected either of the ladies to return for
the wedding. For a moment Archer stood with his eyes fixed on Medora's
fantastic figure, straining to see who came behind her; but the little
procession was at an end, for all the lesser members of the family had
taken their seats, and the eight tall ushers, gathering themselves
together like birds or insects preparing for some migratory manœuvre,
were already slipping through the side doors into the lobby.

"Newland--I say: _she's here!_" the best man whispered.

Archer roused himself with a start.

A long time had apparently passed since his heart had stopped beating,
for the white and rosy procession was in fact half way up the nave, the
Bishop, the Rector and two white-winged assistants were hovering about
the flower-banked altar, and the first chords of the Spohr symphony
were strewing their flower-like notes before the bride.

Archer opened his eyes (but could they really have been shut, as he
imagined?), and felt his heart beginning to resume its usual task. The
music, the scent of the lilies on the altar, the vision of the cloud of
tulle and orange-blossoms floating nearer and nearer, the sight of Mrs.
Archer's face suddenly convulsed with happy sobs, the low benedictory
murmur of the Rector's voice, the ordered evolutions of the eight
pink bridesmaids and the eight black ushers: all these sights, sounds
and sensations, so familiar in themselves, so unutterably strange and
meaningless in his new relation to them, were confusedly mingled in his
brain.

"My God," he thought, "_have_ I got the ring?"--and once more he went
through the bridegroom's convulsive gesture.

Then, in a moment, May was beside him, such radiance streaming from her
that it sent a faint warmth through his numbness, and he straightened
himself and smiled into her eyes.

"Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here," the Rector began ...

The ring was on her hand, the Bishop's benediction had been given,
the bridesmaids were a-poise to resume their place in the procession,
and the organ was showing preliminary symptoms of breaking out into
the Mendelssohn March, without which no newly-wedded couple had ever
emerged upon New York.

"Your arm--_I say, give her your arm!_" young Newland nervously hissed;
and once more Archer became aware of having been adrift far off in the
unknown. What was it that had sent him there, he wondered? Perhaps the
glimpse, among the anonymous spectators in the transept, of a dark coil
of hair under a hat which, a moment later, revealed itself as belonging
to an unknown lady with a long nose, so laughably unlike the person
whose image she had evoked that he asked himself if he were becoming
subject to hallucinations.

And now he and his wife were pacing slowly down the nave, carried
forward on the light Mendelssohn ripples, the spring day beckoning to
them through widely opened doors, and Mrs. Welland's chestnuts, with
big white favours on their frontlets, curvetting and showing off at the
far end of the canvas tunnel.

The footman, who had a still bigger white favour on his lapel, wrapped
May's white cloak about her, and Archer jumped into the brougham at her
side. She turned to him with a triumphant smile and their hands clasped
under her veil.

"Darling!" Archer said--and suddenly the same black abyss yawned before
him and he felt himself sinking into it, deeper and deeper, while his
voice rambled on smoothly and cheerfully: "Yes, of course I thought
I'd lost the ring; no wedding would be complete if the poor devil of
a bridegroom didn't go through that. But you _did_ keep me waiting, you
know! I had time to think of every horror that might possibly happen."

She surprised him by turning, in full Fifth Avenue, and flinging her
arms about his neck. "But none ever can__ happen now, can it, Newland, as
long as we two are together?"


Every detail of the day had been so carefully thought out that the
young couple, after the wedding-breakfast, had ample time to put on
their travelling-clothes, descend the wide Mingott stairs between
laughing bridesmaids and weeping parents, and get into the brougham
under the traditional shower of rice and satin slippers; and there was
still half an hour left in which to drive to the station, buy the last
weeklies at the bookstall with the air of seasoned travellers, and
settle themselves in the reserved compartment in which May's maid had
already placed her dove-coloured travelling cloak and glaringly new
dressing-bag from London.

The old du Lac aunts at Rhinebeck had put their house at the disposal
of the bridal couple, with a readiness inspired by the prospect of
spending a week in New York with Mrs. Archer; and Archer, glad to
escape the usual "bridal suite" in a Philadelphia or Baltimore hotel,
had accepted with an equal alacrity.

May was enchanted at the idea of going to the country, and childishly
amused at the vain efforts of the eight bridesmaids to discover where
their mysterious retreat was situated. It was thought "very English"
to have a country-house lent to one, and the fact gave a last touch of
distinction to what was generally conceded to be the most brilliant
wedding of the year; but where the house was no one was permitted to
know, except the parents of bride and groom, who, when taxed with the
knowledge, pursed their lips and said mysteriously: "Ah, they didn't
tell us--" which was manifestly true, since there was no need to.

Once they were settled in their compartment, and the train, shaking
off the endless wooden suburbs, had pushed out into the pale landscape
of spring, talk became easier than Archer had expected. May was still,
in look and tone, the simple girl of yesterday, eager to compare notes
with him as to the incidents of the wedding, and discussing them as
impartially as a bridesmaid talking it all over with an usher. At first
Archer had fancied that this detachment was the disguise of an inward
tremor; but her clear eyes revealed only the most tranquil unawareness.
She was alone for the first time with her husband; but her husband was
only the charming comrade of yesterday. There was no one whom she liked
as much, no one whom she trusted as completely, and the culminating
"lark" of the whole delightful adventure of engagement and marriage was
to be off with him alone on a journey, like a grownup person, like a
"married woman," in fact.

It was wonderful that--as he had learned in the Mission garden at St.
Augustine--such depths of feeling could coexist with such absence of
imagination. But he remembered how, even then, she had surprised him by
dropping back to inexpressive girlishness as soon as her conscience had
been eased of its burden; and he saw that she would probably go through
life dealing to the best of her ability with each experience as it
came, but never anticipating any by so much as a stolen glance.

Perhaps that faculty of unawareness was what gave her eyes their
transparency, and her face the look of representing a type rather than
a person; as if she might have been chosen to pose for a Civic Virtue
or a Greek goddess. The blood that ran so close to her fair skin might
have been a preserving fluid rather than a ravaging element; yet her
look of indestructible youthfulness made her seem neither hard nor
dull, but only primitive and pure. In the thick of this meditation
Archer suddenly felt himself looking at her with the startled gaze of a
stranger, and plunged into a reminiscence of the wedding-breakfast and
of Granny Mingott's immense and triumphant pervasion of it.

May settled down to frank enjoyment of the subject. "I was surprised,
though--weren't you?--that aunt Medora came after all. Ellen wrote that
they were neither of them well enough to take the journey; I do wish it
had been she who had recovered! Did you see the exquisite old lace she
sent me?"

He had known that the moment must come sooner or later, but he had
somewhat imagined that by force of willing he might hold it at bay.

"Yes--I--no: yes, it was beautiful," he said, looking at her blindly,
and wondering if, whenever he heard those two syllables, all his
carefully built-up world would tumble about him like a house of cards.

"Aren't you tired? It will be good to have some tea when we arrive--I'm
sure the aunts have got everything beautifully ready," he rattled
on, taking her hand in his; and her mind rushed away instantly to
the magnificent tea and coffee service of Baltimore silver which the
Beauforts had sent, and which "went" so perfectly with uncle Lovell
Mingott's trays and side-dishes.

In the spring twilight the train stopped at the Rhinebeck station, and
they walked along the platform to the waiting carriage.

"Ah, how awfully kind of the van der Luydens--they've sent their man
over from Skuytercliff to meet us," Archer exclaimed, as a sedate
person out of livery approached them and relieved the maid of her bags.

"I'm extremely sorry, sir," said this emissary, "that a little
accident has occurred at the Miss du Lacs': a leak in the water-tank.
It happened yesterday, and Mr. van der Luyden, who heard of it this
morning, sent a housemaid up by the early train to get the Patroon's
house ready. It will be quite comfortable, I think you'll find, sir;
and the Miss du Lacs have sent their cook over, so that it will be
exactly the same as if you'd been at Rhinebeck."

Archer stared at the speaker so blankly that he repeated in still more
apologetic accents: "It'll be exactly the same, sir, I do assure you--"
and May's eager voice broke out, covering the embarrassed silence:
"The same as Rhinebeck? The Patroon's house? But it will be a hundred
thousand times better--won't it, Newland? It's too dear and kind of Mr.
van der Luyden to have thought of it."

And as they drove off, with the maid beside the coachman, and their
shining bridal bags on the seat before them, she went on excitedly:
"Only fancy, I've never been inside it--have you? The van der Luydens
show it to so few people. But they opened it for Ellen, it seems, and
she told me what a darling little place it was: she says it's the only
house she's seen in America that she could imagine being perfectly
happy in."

"Well--that's what we're going to be, isn't it?" cried her husband
gaily; and she answered with her boyish smile: "Ah, it's just our luck
beginning--the wonderful luck we're always going to have together!"

The day breathed bright and sharp, a giddy spring wind whipping through Manhattan’s cobblestones, heavy with fine dust and the faint green tang of budding park trees. Every matriarch in the extended Welland and Archer clans had dragged their long-stored furs from cedar chests, sables faded to soft ash and ermines yellowed at the cuffs, so the sharp, heady reek of camphor hanging over Grace Church’s front pews nearly drowned out the delicate, sweet lily scent billowing up from the banked altar flowers.

At the sexton’s quiet signal, Newland Archer stepped out of the vestry to stand beside his best man on the chancel steps, his boots soft on the worn stone. The signal meant the brougham carrying May and her father was just in sight, but he knew there would be a long, fussy stretch of last-minute adjustments in the church lobby, where the bridesmaids hovered already like a cluster of pale Easter blossoms. It was the tradition for the groom to stand exposed to the full gaze of the assembled guests, proof of his eagerness to marry, and Archer submitted to the ritual as resignedly as he had every other absurd, ancient custom that made a 19th century New York wedding feel like a rite pulled straight from the dawn of time. Every step of the path he’d chosen felt equally trivial, equally sharp-edged, and he obeyed his flustered best man’s last-minute instructions as piously as grooms he’d guided through the same labyrinth of rules had obeyed him years before.

He’d checked every box, he was fairly certain. Eight bouquets of white lilac and lily of the valley had been sent to the bridesmaids on time, along with gold-and-sapphire sleeve links for the eight ushers, and a cat’s-eye scarf pin for his best man. He’d sat up half the night the day before rewriting his thank-you notes for the pile of wedding gifts from his male friends and old half-forgotten flirtations. The bishop and rector’s fees were safely tucked in his best man’s pocket, his own travelling bags were already at Mrs. Manson Mingott’s house where the wedding breakfast would be held, and a private compartment had been reserved on the train that would carry him and May off to their secret honeymoon destination – hiding the location of their first night away was one of the most sacred, unbreakable taboos of the old society ritual.

“Got the ring all right?” whispered young van der Luyden Newland, the inexperienced best man, white-knuckled under the weight of his responsibility.

Archer made the familiar gesture he’d seen a hundred other grooms make: he slipped his ungloved right hand into the pocket of his dark grey waistcoat, and felt the tiny warm gold circlet, engraved inside *Newland to May, April ——, 187—*, nestled safely in its velvet case. He settled back into his pose, tall hat and pearl-grey gloves stitched with black held in his left hand, and stared at the church’s heavy oak doors. Overhead, Handel’s wedding march swelled pompously through the imitation stone vaulting, carrying with it the ghost of every other wedding he’d stood witness to in that exact spot, watching other brides drift up the nave to meet other waiting grooms.

“Just like a first night at the Opera,” he thought to himself, recognizing all the same society faces in the same familiar pews, and wondering if the day the Last Trump blew, Mrs. Selfridge Merry would still be perched there wearing that towering ostrich feather bonnet, Mrs. Beaufort still glinting in her diamond earrings with that same unchanging smile, and if they’d already reserved the best proscenium seats in the afterlife.

He had time, still, to scan the first rows of faces one by one: the women sharp with curiosity and giddy excitement, the men sulky and resentful that they’d been forced to squeeze into frock coats before luncheon and fight for plates of food at the breakfast later. “Too bad the breakfast’s at old Catherine’s,” he could almost hear Reggie Chivers grumble. “But I heard Lovell Mingott made them use his own chef, so it ought to be good if you can fight your way to the table.” And Sillerton Jackson would chime right after, all self-important authority: “My dear boy, haven’t you heard? They’re serving it at small little tables, the new English fashion.”

Archer’s gaze softened as it landed on the left-hand pew, where his mother, who’d entered on Henry van der Luyden’s arm, wept softly behind her Chantilly veil, her hands tucked deep in her grandmother’s big ermine muff. Poor Janey, his sister, he thought – even twisting her neck as far as she could, she’d only be able to see the people in the first few pews, all the dowdy, stuffy old Newland and Dagonet relatives. On the near side of the white ribbon marking the family reserved seats, Beaufort stood tall and red-faced, staring boldly out over the crowd of women with his usual arrogant stare. Beside him his wife sat swaddled in silvery chinchilla and pinned with fresh violets, and on the far side of the ribbon, Lawrence Lefferts’s sleekly combed head looked like it was standing guard over the invisible patron saint of “Good Form” that presided over every New York ceremony. Archer wondered how many tiny, unforgivable flaws Lefferts’s sharp eyes would pick out of the day’s ritual, then realized with a faint jolt he’d once cared about those stupid little rules too. All the things that had once filled his days felt like a nursery play-pretend of real life, medieval scholars squabbling over meaningless words no one actually understood. Just the night before, the whole family had had a screaming, hours-long fight over whether to display the wedding presents for guests, and Mrs. Welland had dissolved into indignant tears, swearing she’d “sooner let reporters run loose in my house” than show the gifts off – once upon a time, Archer would have had very strong, very loud opinions on the rightness of that call. Now it all felt absurd.

“And all the while,” he thought, quiet and hollow, “real people were out living real lives somewhere, weren’t they?”

“There they come!” his best man breathed, excited – but Archer knew better. The soft creak of the church door only meant Mr. Brown, the livery stable keeper who doubled as sexton in a black gown, was peeking out to survey the crowd before herding the procession inside. The door clicked shut again, and after another long, breathless interval, it swung wide open. A soft murmur rippled through every pew: “The family!”

Mrs. Welland led the way on her eldest son’s arm, her big pink face appropriately solemn, her plum-colored satin gown with pale blue side panels and blue ostrich plumes in her small bonnet earning quiet nods of approval from the crowd. But before she could settle with a great stately rustle into the pew across from Archer’s mother, every head was craning to see who came next. Wild rumors had run through the clubs the day before: old Mrs. Manson Mingott, despite her crippling weight and bad legs, was determined to be at the ceremony. The bets had run high – would she make it up the nave? She’d even sent her own carpenter over to measure the front pew, to see if they could saw off the end panel to make space for her, and for a whole day the family had watched her toy with the plan of being wheeled up the whole aisle in her massive Bath chair, enthroned right at the foot of the chancel. The whole family had been desperate to avoid that undignified spectacle, and they’d nearly handed a fortune to the servant who’d suddenly pointed out the Bath chair was too wide to fit through the iron supports of the awning that stretched from the church doors to the curb. Old Catherine had weighed tearing the awning down for half a second, but the thought of the crowds of dressmakers and newspaper reporters jostling outside, of them taking photographs of the wedding to print in the papers, had made the whole clan recoil in collective horror. Catherine had conceded to skip the church service – but only on the hard promise that the wedding breakfast would be held at her house.

Even after all that, a small group of betting holdouts still swore she’d make a surprise appearance, and a soft huff of disappointment ran through the crowd when they saw her daughter-in-law walk in instead. Then came the gaunt, mincing figure of Medora Manson, swathed in a wild mess of stripes, fringes, and floating scarves – and Archer’s heart seized up so tight he thought it might stop beating. He’d been certain Medora and Ellen Olenska were still in Washington, that they’d left four weeks earlier to get Medora away from the cult leader Dr. Agathon Carver who’d almost recruited her for his “Valley of Love” commune. No one had expected either of them to come back for the wedding. He stared hard at Medora’s strange, frilly figure, craning to see who was right behind her – but the little procession was already over. There was no one else. Ellen wasn’t there.

“Newland – I say, she’s here!” his best man hissed in his ear.

Archer jolted back to his senses. Time had slipped away on him, he realized, because the pale pink bridesmaid procession was already halfway up the nave, the bishop, rector, and two white-robed acolytes hovering by the lily-heavy altar, and the first soft chords of the Spohr symphony were spilling like scattered petals ahead of the bride. He blinked, and the blur of tulle and orange blossoms that was May drifted closer and closer. She was glowing, so bright she sent a faint soft warmth through all his cold numbness, and he straightened up, and smiled right into her eyes as she came to stand beside him.

“Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here,” the rector began.

The ring slid onto her finger. The bishop gave his final benediction. The bridesmaids shifted to fall back into line, and the organ started rumbling the first notes of the Mendelssohn march – the one no New York newlywed couple had ever walked out of the church without. “Your arm! Give her your arm!” young Newland the best man hissed, nervous as a cat, and Archer realized he’d drifted off somewhere far away, half-convinced he’d caught a glimpse of Ellen’s dark coiled hair in the crowd of onlookers, only for it to turn out to be a total stranger with a long nose, so absurdly different he wondered if he was starting to hallucinate.

He and May walked slowly down the nave together, carried along on the light ripples of the march, the bright spring day beckoning through the wide open church doors. The footman wrapped her soft white cloak around her, and Archer jumped into the brougham right beside her. May turned to him with a brilliant, triumphant smile, and their hands clasped tight under her veil.

“Darling,” Archer said – and for a split second that dark, empty abyss yawned open under his feet, and he felt himself falling, falling, even as his voice came out smooth and cheerful, light as air. “Of course I thought I’d lost the ring. No wedding is complete without the poor groom panicking over that. But you did keep me waiting, you know! I had time to imagine every terrible disaster that could possibly happen.”

To his shock, she threw her arms around his neck right there in full view of Fifth Avenue’s passersby. “But none of them can ever happen now, can it Newland? Not as long as we’re together.”

Every last detail of the day had been planned to perfection. After the wedding breakfast, they had plenty of time to change into their travelling clothes, walk down Mrs. Mingott’s wide staircase between grinning bridesmaids and weeping parents, and climb into their brougham under the traditional shower of thrown rice and satin slippers. They still had half an hour left to drive to the station, buy the latest weeklies at the bookstall like two seasoned, experienced travellers, and settle into their private compartment, where May’s maid had already stowed her dove-grey travelling cloak and the brand new, shining leather dressing bag she’d ordered all the way from London. The old du Lac aunts out in Rhinebeck had lent them their country house for the honeymoon, eager to spend a week in New York visiting Archer’s mother, and Archer had jumped at the chance, glad to skip the usual dreadful bridal suite in a Philadelphia or Baltimore hotel. May was over the moon about the country, giggling at the way the eight bridesmaids had run around trying and failing to find out their secret retreat’s location. It was deemed “very English” to have a friend lend you a country house, and it made the wedding the most talked-about, brilliant event of the whole year.

Once the train pulled out of the city, shaking off the endless stretches of wooden suburban houses to roll out into pale, greening spring countryside, talking came easier to Archer than he’d expected. May was still the bright, simple, uncomplicated girl he’d fallen in love with, gushing to him over every little silly detail of the wedding, as casual and unshaken as if she was just chatting over tea. At first he’d thought her calmness was just a mask for jittery nerves, but her clear, wide eyes held nothing but unclouded, happy innocence. She was alone for the first time with her husband – but her husband was just her favorite, most trusted comrade, and this whole great adventure of running off on a journey together was the most fun, most wonderful lark she could possibly imagine. It amazed him, that such soft, deep warmth could exist in someone with no imagination at all – no quiet, secret hunger for the things they weren’t supposed to want.

“ I was surprised, though – weren’t you? – that Aunt Medora turned up after all,” May said suddenly, pulling him out of his thoughts. “Ellen wrote that neither of them were well enough to make the journey. I do wish it had been Ellen who felt well enough to come! Did you see the exquisite old lace she sent me as a wedding gift?”

Archer had known this moment would come eventually, but he’d foolishly thought he could will it away. “Yes – I – it was beautiful,” he said, staring at her blindly, wondering if every time he heard Ellen’s name his whole carefully constructed, carefully normal world would tumble down around him like a house of cards. “Aren’t you tired? It’ll be so nice to have tea when we get to the house, I’m sure the aunts have everything perfectly ready,” he rattled on, grabbing her hand tight in his. She instantly switched tracks, chattering excitedly about the magnificent Baltimore silver tea and coffee service the Beauforts had gifted them, how perfectly it matched the trays Lovell Mingott had given them.

The train pulled into the Rhinebeck station as the spring twilight deepened, and they walked along the platform to the waiting carriage. “Ah, how kind of the van der Luydens,” Archer exclaimed, spotting the sedate, unliveried man waiting by their bags. “They sent their man all the way over from Skuytercliff to meet us.”

“I’m very sorry, sir,” the man said, apologetic. “There was a little accident at the Misses du Lac’s house yesterday – their water tank sprung a leak. Mr. van der Luyden heard about it first thing this morning, and sent a housemaid up on the early train to get the Patroon’s house ready for you instead. It’s perfectly comfortable, sir, I promise you – and the Misses du Lac sent their cook over too, so it will be exactly the same as if you were staying in Rhinebeck.”

Archer stared at him blankly. May broke in before he could speak, bright and excited. “The same as Rhinebeck? The Patroon’s house? That’s a hundred thousand times better! Isn’t it, Newland? It’s the dearest, kindest thing Mr. van der Luyden could have done for us.” She leaned forward, giddy, as the carriage pulled away, their shiny new bridal bags on the seat in front of them. “I’ve never been inside it – have you? The van der Luydens barely ever show it to anyone. But they opened it for Ellen once, you know. She told me what a darling little place it was – she said it’s the only house in all of America she could ever imagine being perfectly happy in.”

“Well, that’s what we’re going to be, isn’t it?” Archer said, laughing, bright and easy, and she smiled that boyish, uncomplicated smile of hers.

“Ah!” she said. “This is our luck starting, isn’t it? The wonderful, perfect luck we’re going to have together, always.”
